q: How does vineyard aspect influence ripening in a cool region?
opts: North-facing slopes always ripen fastest in the Northern Hemisphere
It has no measurable effect on the temperature of the fruit
Aspect only affects drainage, not the warmth of the site
Slopes angled toward the sun receive more direct energy
exp: A slope tilted toward the sun intercepts light closer to perpendicular and warms more. In the Northern Hemisphere that means south-facing sites in marginal climates.

q: Which soil property is generally most important for quality viticulture?
opts: High fertility
High clay content
Good drainage
Dark colour
exp: Vines do well on poor, well-drained soil that forces roots down and limits vigour. Rich, wet soil tends to give abundant leafy growth and diluted fruit.

q: The large rounded stones known as galets are most associated with which area?
opts: Willamette Valley
Barossa Valley
Chateauneuf-du-Pape
Chablis
exp: Galets are the rounded quartzite cobbles across parts of Chateauneuf-du-Pape. They store daytime heat and release it overnight, and they slow evaporation.

q: Slate soils are most closely identified with which region?
opts: Napa Valley
Loire Valley
Mosel
Barossa Valley
exp: The Mosel's steep slate slopes hold heat and shed water. Dark slate warming in the sun is part of how such a northerly region ripens Riesling at all.

q: What does the term terroir describe?
opts: A style of oak barrel traditionally used for maturing red wine
A legally defined bottle shape reserved to one region
A method of pruning that trains the vine along a wire
The natural environment of a site and its mark on the wine
exp: Terroir gathers soil, subsoil, climate, topography and aspect into the idea that a place leaves a recognisable signature in its wine.

q: Why are limestone and chalk soils valued in cool regions?
opts: They drain well yet hold reserve moisture
They eliminate the need for rootstock
They prevent all fungal disease
They feed sugar directly into the ripening fruit
exp: Chalk and limestone drain freely but retain water in their pores, giving vines a buffer in dry spells without waterlogging them.

q: What is the main purpose of canopy management?
opts: To raise the alcohol of the finished wine
To increase the number of buds the vine carries into spring
To balance sunlight and airflow around the fruit
To stop the graft union failing in its first years
exp: Positioning shoots and removing selected leaves gets light onto the fruit and air through the bunches, aiding ripening and reducing fungal pressure.

q: What distinguishes cane pruning from spur pruning?
opts: Cane pruning keeps long canes, spur pruning short spurs
There is no structural difference; the two words are interchangeable
Cane pruning is used only on white varieties, spur pruning only on red
Cane pruning is done in summer and spur pruning in winter
exp: Cane pruning keeps long one-year-old wood laid along a wire; spur pruning keeps short spurs on a permanent cordon. The choice affects vigour and frost exposure.

q: Green harvest refers to which practice?
opts: Picking the whole crop before the grapes have coloured
Dropping unripe bunches to concentrate the rest
Harvesting at night so the fruit reaches the winery cool
Planting a green cover crop between the rows
exp: Cutting away a share of the crop at or near veraison directs the vine's resources into fewer bunches. It is a quality lever, and a costly one.

q: In general, what is the relationship between very high yields and wine concentration?
opts: Yield has no bearing on concentration
Higher yields tend to reduce concentration
Yield affects only colour
Higher yields always increase concentration
exp: Spreading a vine's capacity across more fruit usually dilutes it. This is why quality appellations cap yields, though site and vine balance matter as much as the number.

q: What distinguishes biodynamic viticulture from organic viticulture?
opts: Biodynamics permits synthetic pesticides that organic rules forbid
There is no difference; the two certifications cover the same rules
Biodynamics forbids all ploughing and any work on the soil
Biodynamics adds preparations and a lunar calendar
exp: Biodynamic growing is organic at its base, then adds specific preparations and a lunar and astronomical calendar drawn from Steiner's lectures.

q: What is the principal advantage of hand harvesting over machine harvesting?
opts: Pickers can select, and whole bunches stay intact
It is required by law for all red wine
It is always faster than a machine over the same area
It removes any need to sort the fruit at the winery
exp: Hands can choose what to take and leave, and deliver whole undamaged bunches. Machines are quicker and cheaper, and can pick cool at night, but they shake fruit free.

q: In many traditional European regions, irrigation is restricted primarily because
opts: it damages rootstock
it can inflate yields
water is unavailable
it is impossible on slopes
exp: Withholding water keeps vines moderately stressed and berries small, and watering to push the crop up dilutes what is in the berries. Regions with reliable rainfall have tended to treat irrigation as a route to volume rather than quality.

q: Higher vine planting density is generally intended to achieve what?
opts: Competition between the vines
A longer dormancy through the winter
Easier passage for machines between the rows
Larger berries and heavier bunches
exp: Crowding vines makes them compete for water and nutrients, restraining each one. It suits poor soils, and it raises the cost of establishing and working the vineyard.

q: Phylloxera is what kind of organism?
opts: A soil-borne fungus
A bacterium
A virus
A root-feeding aphid
exp: Phylloxera is a tiny aphid that feeds on vinifera roots, and it devastated European vineyards from the later nineteenth century. Grafting remains the answer.

q: Which pair are the two most significant fungal diseases of the vine?
opts: Esca and eutypa
Botrytis and phylloxera
Chlorosis and coulure
Powdery and downy mildew
exp: Powdery mildew (oidium) and downy mildew (peronospora) are the chronic fungal threats, both arriving from North America in the nineteenth century.
